title: Delhi's Winter Pollution Curbs Are Back. Four Winters of Data Question Them
excerpt: A CREA analysis finds Delhi's average winter AQI rose from 280 in 2022-23 to 295 in 2025-26 despite GRAP restrictions on nearly four in five winter days — though a separate official-linked study says the curbs prevented far worse air.
body:
• Delhi's average winter Air Quality Index rose from 280 in 2022-23 to 295 in 2025-26, according to a Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) analysis.
  • Nearly 80% of winter days were under Stage II GRAP restrictions or higher — emergency measures have become the normal state, not the exception.
  • In 10 of 12 severe episodes CREA studied, pollution worsened in the week after Delhi entered GRAP Stage III or IV.
  • A separate study by IITM Pune and CAQM scientists estimates that without GRAP, Delhi could have faced about 60% more hours of severe air — the curbs may blunt peaks without fixing the trend.

Delhi's winter pollution curbs are back, as they are every year. The harder question, now backed by four winters of data, is whether the emergency system behind them is improving the air at all.

An analysis by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) found that Delhi's average winter Air Quality Index rose from 280 in 2022-23 to 295 in 2025-26, despite restrictions imposed through four winter seasons under the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP), according to Mirror Now's report of the findings. Nearly four in five winter days saw restrictions under Stage II of GRAP or higher.

Emergency mode, permanently

GRAP is a graded system: restrictions on construction, traffic, industry and other sources intensify across four stages as pollution worsens, and since a 2022 revision the stages can be triggered on forecasts rather than after the air has already turned severe. It is designed as an emergency brake — a way to limit exposure during dangerous episodes — not as a year-round emissions-control programme.

https://x.com/CNBCTV18News/status/2114718290383892805

CREA examined 12 episodes in which Delhi's AQI rose from below Stage III to Stage III or IV, three in each of four winters. In 10 of the 12, pollution worsened in the week after the city entered the severe stages, The CSR Journal reported. The sharpest rise came after November 2, 2023, when the AQI increased by 114 points, from 317 to 431.

The counter-argument

That does not prove the curbs do nothing. A separate study by scientists from the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology, Pune, and the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) suggests GRAP may have mitigated pollution levels — estimating that without its restrictions, Delhi could have faced about 60% more hours of severe air quality, with significantly more instances of AQI exceeding 300. On that reading, GRAP blunts the worst peaks even while the average keeps drifting up, because the underlying sources across the wider region keep operating.

What this means for residents and visitors

Both findings can be true at once, and together they set expectations for this winter: expect Stage II or higher restrictions on most days from November to February, plan outdoor activity around daily AQI readings rather than the calendar, and treat the curbs as exposure management, not a fix. Lasting improvement, the CREA analysis argues, requires cutting the year-round regional sources — vehicles, industry, dust and crop-residue smoke — that an emergency plan switched on in October cannot reach.
